recipe: Beef & stout stew with parsley suet dumplings
servesNote: 2½ portions — Karl 3 : Maria 2. Dumplings scaled to FOUR, which is what the shop bought and what the card recommends cooking tonight.
adaptations: ⭐ DUMPLINGS, confirmed by Karl. The shop bought 32 g suet and 70 g flour — exactly the card's 110:50 ratio at 64%, which is FOUR dumplings rather than six. That matches the card's own advice: dumplings do not survive reheating, so roll what you will eat tonight. Quantities below are already scaled.
The 25 g dredging flour is not on the cart because it comes from the 500 g of held plain flour (BB Oct 2026). This dish is the reason that flour has a job at all, and it uses it twice.
320 g of potatoes were also bought. The card treats potatoes as the dumpling-free alternative — you have both, so they are a side if you want one, not a substitute.

ingredients.prep: ⭐ HOLD BACK 60 ml of it for the very end
from the held 500 g — a bloom you can barely see, not a batter
use the earliest best-before pack — one is dated 03/09

equipment.why: browns on the hob, then goes in the oven for three hours
150°C / 130°C fan for the braise, then up to 190°C / 170°C fan for the dumplings
dredging the beef, then the dumpling dough
scraping the fond to bare metal
cutting the water through the dumpling dough — a spoon overworks it
patting the beef dry — wet meat will not brown

prep: Beef out of the fridge while you prep. Fridge-cold meat dropped into hot fat seizes and toughens.
Cut the beef to a rough 4 cm — big chunks, so they survive three hours — and pat every piece thoroughly dry.
Thickly slice the onion, cut the carrots into thick diagonal chunks, slice the celery.
Make up the chicken stock sachet to 300 ml.
⚠️ Open the stout and MEASURE 60 ml back into the can straight away. It is far too easy to tip the lot in, and timing — not quantity — is what makes a stout stew bitter.

steps.text: 25 g flour, salt and plenty of pepper in a bowl. Turn the beef until every piece is lightly and evenly dusted, then lift out and shake off the excess. A thick coat goes pasty and can scorch; a thin one dries the surface, browns alongside the meat, and dissolves into the gravy so you never need a slurry later.

Oil in the casserole over medium-high until it shimmers. Brown in two or three batches, single layer with gaps, turning only once each side has a deep brown crust that releases from the pan by itself. Touching pieces cool the pan, the meat weeps, and you boil grey beef in its own juice. Each batch out, juices kept.

Medium heat. Onion, carrots, celery, a pinch of salt, scraping constantly until the onion is translucent with golden edges and the brown crust on the base has lifted into the vegetables and the metal is clean again. That fond is a large fraction of the flavour, and the water coming out of the vegetables is the tool that gets it off.
Push the vegetables aside. Tomato paste onto the bare hot base until it darkens from bright red to brick, then the roasted garlic paste for about 30 seconds, until it smells sweet.

⭐ HALF the stout, boiled hard, scraping until nothing sticks to the pan. Most recipes say 'add the beer' as one action; deglazing while the pan is at its hottest is the difference. Then the rest of it — keeping the 60 ml back — plus the stock, bay, thyme, balsamic, sugar and Worcestershire.

Beef and its juices back in. Liquid about three-quarters up the meat, not covering it — exposed tops concentrate, and the whole thing reduces to gravy rather than soup. Bring it to where the surface just shivers with the occasional bubble, never a rolling boil. Boiling squeezes water out faster than collagen turns to gelatin, which gives you meat that is falling apart and dry at the same time.

Lid on, into the oven at 150°C / 130°C fan. Ready when a piece crushes against the side of the pot under light pressure from a spoon, with no springiness at all. ⚠️ If it still resists it is not overcooked, it is undercooked — give it another 30 minutes.

Dumplings — make them any time while it braises, the dough sits happily in the fridge. Flour, baking powder, salt and suet stirred together, then the parsley. Cold water a splash at a time, cutting it through with a knife, until it just comes together into a soft, slightly craggy dough that holds when squeezed but is not sticky. DO NOT KNEAD IT — working suet dough develops gluten and melts the suet into the flour. You want the suet still visible as flecks, because each fleck melts in the oven and leaves a steam pocket. Roll four balls with floured hands.

Casserole out, lid off. Oven up to 190°C / 170°C fan. Stir in the reserved 60 ml of stout. Taste: it should be savoury and faintly sweet with a bittersweet edge, not sour or harsh. Too thin? Bubble it uncovered until a spoon dragged across the base leaves a channel that fills in slowly.

Dumplings on top, spaced apart and only HALF-submerged. Back in UNCOVERED. Done when they have visibly risen, the tops are dry, pale-golden and slightly crusted, and a skewer comes out clean. Uncovered is deliberate — bottoms steam in the gravy, tops dry and crisp. Covered, they go uniformly wet.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat. The gravy thickens noticeably as it stops boiling.
